title: Serve an LLM Feature with FastAPI in Production and Defend It

teaser.setup: You're building the API that fronts an LLM/model for a real product. Design the FastAPI service and defend it under pressure — async, streaming, resilience, backpressure, and observability.
you_will_practice: Async I/O and streaming responses for model calls
Timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, and fallbacks
Backpressure, load shedding, and concurrency limits

sample_node.prompt: Why async endpoints here instead of a simple synchronous handler?
sample_node.model: LLM/model calls are I/O-bound and slow (hundreds of ms to seconds). Sync handlers tie up a worker per in-flight request, so a handful of slow calls starve the pool and throughput collapses. Async + httpx lets one worker await many upstream calls concurrently. Trade-off: async code is easier to get subtly wrong (blocking calls sneak in), so you keep CPU work off the event loop.

n1.prompt: Clarify first, then give your one-paragraph design for a FastAPI service fronting an LLM.
n1.model: Clarify: expected QPS, p95 latency target, response size/streaming need, and the upstream model's limits. Design: async endpoints with httpx to the model; Pydantic request validation; stream long generations via SSE; per-call timeouts, bounded retries with backoff + a circuit breaker, and a fallback (cheaper/cached answer); concurrency limits + load shedding; structured logs with request IDs; health/readiness probes. Long jobs go to a task queue, not the request worker.

n2.prompt: Why async endpoints here instead of a simple synchronous handler?
n2.model: Model calls are I/O-bound and slow, so sync ties up a worker per in-flight request and a few slow calls starve the pool — throughput collapses. Async + httpx lets one worker await many upstream calls concurrently. Trade-off: it's easy to accidentally block the event loop, so CPU work and blocking libraries must be offloaded.

n3.prompt: The model provider gets slow and flaky at peak. How does your service stay up?
n3.model: Per-call timeout so a slow upstream can't hang a request; bounded retries with exponential backoff + jitter (not retry-forever); a circuit breaker that fails fast when the provider is down; and a fallback — an alternate provider/region, a cheaper model, or a cached/graceful answer. Multi-provider config to prevent a single point of failure. Mitigate now (breaker/fallback) and prevent (failover).

n4.prompt: A traffic spike arrives. How do you prevent the service from collapsing?
n4.model: Backpressure: a bounded concurrency limit and a queue with a max wait; when full, shed load with 429 + Retry-After instead of accepting work you can't finish. A fast 429 protects the healthy path and the upstream from a thundering herd. Scale horizontally behind a load balancer; keep streaming connections accounted for in the concurrency budget. Protect, then scale.

n5.prompt: p95 latency doubled in prod but the model provider looks fine. Diagnose it.
n5.model: Instrument the request end to end: time spent in validation, queueing/backpressure wait, upstream call, and serialization/streaming. Common causes: an accidental blocking call on the event loop, connection-pool exhaustion to the model (raise/limit pool, keep-alive), GC/CPU from large payloads, or queue wait under load. Use the traces/request IDs to localize the stage, then fix that stage — don't blanket-scale.
signals: end-to-end tracing to localize the stage

n6.prompt: Where did you assert a choice without the mechanism, the trade-off, or the verification?
checklist: I justified async by the I/O-bound workload
I handled spikes with backpressure + load shedding
I made it observable (traces/request IDs) to diagnose latency
